children: Hyundai Motor (HYMLF) CEO Jose Munoz is warning that Chinese automakers could rapidly pressure the U.S. car market if Washington loosens tariffs and other trade protections, pointing to Europe as a preview of what could happen.

Munoz said Chinese vehicles are priced roughly 30% to 40% below competing models in markets including Italy, Spain and France, despite European Union trade barriers such as tariffs and minimum-price commitments.
The pricing gap has helped Chinese brands gain significant ground abroad.
The U.K., which does not impose comparable tariffs on Chinese vehicles, offers an even starker example, according to Munoz.
"So I think we could expect similar things to happen in the U.S., at different levels, unless there are certain conditions," he warned.
The U.S. has effectively kept Chinese electric vehicles out of the market through tariffs of roughly 100%.
But the competitive debate could change if Chinese manufacturers begin building cars domestically.
President Donald Trump recently said he would be open to Chinese automakers manufacturing vehicles in the U.S. as long as they employ American workers.
Munoz is not alone in warning about the potential disruption.
Ford (F) CEO Jim Farley told employees in July that the company was preparing for the possibility that Chinese automakers could enter the U.S. market within the next five to 10 years.

If Chinese automakers eventually enter the U.S. with vehicles priced materially below domestic and foreign rivals, established manufacturers could be forced to cut prices, spend more aggressively on technology or accept lower margins.
That would create pressure not only for Hyundai, but potentially Ford and other mass-market automakers competing in EVs and lower-priced vehicles.
Tariffs currently provide an important buffer.
But investors should watch whether U.S. policy shifts from blocking Chinese imports toward encouraging local production.
That could preserve American manufacturing jobs while still introducing much tougher competition.
For automakers already dealing with EV investment costs and uneven demand, a new wave of lower-priced Chinese vehicles could make the industry's margin challenge considerably harder.

title: Hyundai CEO Sends Warning on Chinese Cars
